title: How to Make a Gin & Tonic That Doesn’t Taste Flat
subtitle: Simple only works when the ingredients pull their weight.
summary:
A Gin & Tonic looks like the easiest drink in the world, which is exactly why people stop paying attention. Gin, tonic, ice, lime — done. Except not really.

Because tonic makes up most of the drink, it can either make the cocktail feel crisp and alive or dull and overly sweet. If your Gin & Tonic tastes flat, the tonic is usually the first place I’d look.

quick_mix.headline: Quick Mix
lines: Garnish with lime or citrus peel

editorial_sections.title: Tonic Is Not Just Filler
editorial_sections.body: This is where people get lazy. Tonic ↗ is most of the drink, so if it is too sweet, flat, or dull, the whole thing suffers. A good tonic keeps the drink crisp and gives the gin something to work with.

editorial_sections.title: Choose the Gin on Purpose
editorial_sections.body:
A citrus-forward gin makes the drink brighter. A more herbal gin gives it more depth. Neither is wrong, but they create very different drinks.

The point is to choose intentionally instead of just grabbing whatever bottle is closest.

editorial_sections.title: Ice Still Matters
editorial_sections.body: A Gin & Tonic should stay cold and lively. If the ice ↗ melts too quickly, the drink gets watery before you’re halfway through it. Use plenty of solid ice and build the drink directly in the glass.

editorial_sections.title: What a Good Gin & Tonic Should Feel Like
editorial_sections.body:
It should feel crisp, cold, lightly bitter, and refreshing. The gin should still be present, but the tonic should carry the drink without flattening it.

When it’s right, it tastes simple in the best possible way.

steps: Fill a highball glass with plenty of ice.
Garnish with lime or citrus peel.
notes: Use fresh, well-carbonated tonic. If the drink tastes flat or overly sweet, change the tonic before blaming the gin.
